subject: English
name: English Advanced, Year 11
about: HSC, Reading to write, narratives and literature
syllabus: NSW English Advanced 11-12 Syllabus (2024), Year 11 focus areas

points.title: Imagery
points.brief: Language that appeals to the senses so a reader can see, hear, smell, taste or feel a scene. Teach how a writer uses it to place the reader inside an experience.

points.title: Metaphor and simile
points.brief: A simile compares two things using like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another. Both carry ideas from one thing to another, and an extended metaphor runs through a passage.

points.title: Personification and symbolism
points.brief: Personification gives human qualities to something that is not human. A symbol is an object, colour or image that stands for a larger idea, and gains meaning each time it returns.

points.title: Sound devices
points.brief: Alliteration repeats first consonant sounds, assonance repeats vowel sounds, and onomatopoeia imitates a sound. Teach that sound changes pace and mood, not just how a line sounds.

points.title: Tone and mood
points.brief: Tone is the writer's attitude, shown through word choice. Mood is the feeling the text creates in the reader. Students should name a tone precisely, such as wry, bitter or tender.

points.title: Sentence structure and syntax
points.brief: Short sentences can create tension or emphasis. Long, layered sentences can slow the reader or build momentum. Fragments, lists and inverted word order each shape how an idea lands.

points.title: Purpose, audience and context
points.brief: Every text is shaped by why it was written, who it is for, and when and where it was made. These three questions explain most of a writer's choices.

points.title: Imaginative, persuasive and informative texts
points.brief: Imaginative texts tell stories or create worlds, persuasive texts argue for a view, and informative texts explain. Many texts blend purposes, such as a feature article that informs and persuades.

points.title: Discursive writing
points.brief: A discursive text explores an idea from several angles without needing to win an argument. It is reflective, often personal, and can end on a question rather than a firm conclusion.

points.title: Register and diction
points.brief: Register is how formal or informal the language is. Diction is the particular choice of words. Both signal the writer's relationship with the reader.

points.title: Point of view and voice
points.brief: First, second and third person each give a different closeness to events. Voice is the distinct personality a reader hears in the writing, built from diction, rhythm and attitude.

points.title: Learning from a mentor text
points.brief: Reading a short published piece closely to borrow one technique for your own writing, such as its opening move, its structure or its use of a recurring image.

points.title: Showing through detail
points.brief: Specific, concrete details let readers infer a feeling instead of being told it. A clenched jaw shows anger more strongly than the word angry.

points.title: Openings and endings
points.brief: An opening hooks the reader and sets up voice and expectation. An ending can resolve, circle back to the opening, or leave a deliberate question. Both are planned, not left to chance.

points.title: Drafting and editing
points.brief: Drafting gets ideas down. Revising changes structure and meaning. Editing fixes sentences and words. Strong writers cut words that add nothing.

points.title: Narrative structure
points.brief: Many stories move through an orientation, a complication, rising tension, a climax and a resolution. Writers bend this shape with flashbacks, frame stories or endings that stay open.

points.title: Characterisation
points.brief: Writers build characters through what they say, do and think, how others react to them, and direct description. A dynamic character changes over the story; a static one does not.

points.title: Setting and atmosphere
points.brief: Setting is the time and place of a story. It can mirror a character's state, create atmosphere, or act almost like a character itself.

points.title: Narrators and reliability
points.brief: A narrator can be inside or outside the story, all-knowing or limited. An unreliable narrator gives an account the reader learns not to trust, which invites closer reading.

points.title: Archetypes and story patterns
points.brief: Recurring characters and plots, such as the hero's journey, the trickster or the fall from grace, appear across cultures. Writers use them to meet or overturn a reader's expectations.

points.title: Narratives across cultures and time
points.brief: Societies have always told stories to pass on knowledge, values and identity, from oral myths and fables to novels and films. Narratives carry the beliefs of the culture that tells them.

points.title: Narratives in many forms
points.brief: A story can be told in prose, poetry, film, graphic novels, podcasts, games and social media. Each form has its own tools, such as camera angles in film or panels in a graphic novel.

points.title: How narratives shape values
points.brief: Stories reward some behaviours and punish others, and invite readers to admire or judge characters. Over time this shapes what a community sees as normal or right.

points.title: Retelling and reimagining stories
points.brief: Writers retell older stories to question them, update them for a new audience or give a voice to a character who was silent. Comparing versions shows what each one values.

points.title: Counter-narratives
points.brief: A counter-narrative tells a story from a perspective the dominant story left out, challenging who is seen as the hero and whose experience counts.

points.title: Comparing two narratives
points.brief: Putting two stories side by side to see how their forms, contexts and values differ. A good comparison explains why the differences matter, not only what they are.

points.title: Analysing a narrative technique
points.brief: Naming a technique, giving a brief example in your own words or a short quote, and explaining its effect on the reader and its link to the text's ideas.

points.title: Writing your own narrative
points.brief: Using what was learned from studying narratives to write one, choosing a narrator, a structure and a central image that carry a clear idea.

points.title: Form and genre conventions
points.brief: Form is the kind of text (novel, play, poem, film). Genre is a type of story with expected features, such as gothic or dystopian. Writers follow and break these conventions to make meaning.

points.title: Context of composition
points.brief: The historical, social and personal circumstances in which a text was written. Context helps explain a text's concerns, but the text is more than a record of its time.

points.title: Context of reception
points.brief: Readers in different times and places bring their own values to a text, so the same text can be read differently in 1900 and today. This is why interpretations shift.

points.title: Structure across a whole text
points.brief: How a text is ordered as a whole, through chapters, acts, stanzas or scenes, and how that order builds tension, contrast or a final effect.

points.title: Motifs and recurring images
points.brief: A motif is an image, phrase or idea that returns through a text. Tracing it shows how the text develops its ideas from start to finish.

points.title: Readings and interpretations
points.brief: An interpretation is an argued view of what a text means. More than one reading can be valid, but each must be supported by close evidence from the text.

points.title: Supporting a reading with evidence
points.brief: Choosing short, precise quotations or references, and explaining how each one supports the argument. Evidence without analysis does not prove anything.

points.title: Why some texts endure
points.brief: Texts that are studied for generations often explore lasting human questions, use language with unusual skill, and reward rereading. Students can argue what makes a text worth studying.

points.title: Writing a thesis
points.brief: A thesis is a clear, arguable answer to the question in one or two sentences. It names an idea about the text, not just a topic, and the whole essay sets out to prove it.

points.title: Topic sentences
points.brief: Each body paragraph opens with a sentence that states one step of the argument and links back to the thesis and the question.

points.title: Embedding evidence
points.brief: Weaving short quotations into your own sentences so they read smoothly, instead of dropping in long quotes on their own.

points.title: Technique, example and effect
points.brief: A basic analytical move. Name the technique, give the example, then explain its effect and how it supports the argument. The effect is where most marks are earned.

points.title: Conclusions
points.brief: A conclusion restates the thesis in fresh words, draws the argument together and may show why it matters. It adds no new evidence.
